md: The ray arriving is the **incident ray**; the ray leaving is the **reflected ray**. Where they meet the mirror you draw the **normal**: a dashed line at **right angles to the mirror**. The rule is short: the **angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection**, and both angles sit between a ray and the normal.

stem: A ray strikes a plane mirror with an angle of incidence of 27°. State the angle of reflection, and draw the reflected ray. [3]

steps.working: Draw the normal, dashed, at right angles to the mirror where the ray lands.
steps.decision: Both angles are measured from it, so it goes on first.

steps.working: Angle of reflection = angle of incidence = 27°.
steps.decision: The law of reflection: the two angles are equal.

steps.working: Draw the reflected ray at 27° on the other side of the normal, with an arrow pointing away from the mirror.
steps.decision: Measure with a protractor from the normal; the arrow carries a mark.

prompt: A ray hits a plane mirror with an angle of incidence of 48°. What is the angle of reflection, in degrees?
explain: 48°. The two angles are equal, both measured from the normal, so once you have the angle of incidence there is nothing to work out.

twin.prompt: A ray strikes a plane mirror with an angle of reflection of 33°. What was its angle of incidence, in degrees?
twin.explain: The law works both ways: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, so it was 33°.

md: A diagram will sometimes mark the angle **between the ray and the mirror surface**. That is not the angle of incidence. The mirror and the normal are at right angles, so the two angles add to **90°**: subtract the printed angle from 90° first.

title: Why the normal, and not the mirror?
md: Because the normal is the one line that behaves the same way for every surface, flat or curved. Measuring from the normal lets the same rule describe a flat mirror, a curved mirror and, later, refraction through glass. Draw the normal first and every angle question in optics becomes the same question.

stem: A ray meets a plane mirror at 22° to the mirror surface. Find the angle of reflection. [3]

steps.working: Draw the normal at right angles to the mirror where the ray lands.
steps.decision: The printed angle is to the mirror, so the normal is needed to find the right one.
The mirror and the normal are at right angles, so subtract from 90°.

steps.working: angle of reflection = angle of incidence = 68°
steps.decision: Now the law of reflection, on the correct angle.

prompt: A ray meets a mirror at 36° to the mirror surface. What is the angle of incidence, in degrees?
explain: 90° − 36° = 54°. The printed angle is to the mirror; the angle of incidence is to the normal, which is at right angles to the mirror.

twin.prompt: A ray meets a mirror at 17° to the mirror surface. What is the angle of incidence, in degrees?
twin.explain: 90° − 17° = 73°: draw the normal, then subtract the printed angle from 90°.

md: Rays from an object reflect and enter your eye. Your brain assumes light travels in straight lines, so it traces them back to a point **behind** the mirror: the **image**. No light ever reaches it, so the image is **virtual**. It is the **same size** as the object, **upright**, and **behind** the mirror by the same distance the object stands in front.

stem: A candle stands 9 cm in front of a plane mirror. Describe its image, and say where it is. [4]

steps.working: Virtual: the light only seems to come from behind the mirror.
steps.decision: No light passes through the mirror, so nothing is really there.

steps.working: Upright and the same size as the candle.
steps.decision: A flat mirror neither turns the image over nor changes its size.

steps.working: Laterally inverted: its left and right are swapped.
steps.decision: The full phrase; inverted alone would mean upside down.
The mirror sits exactly halfway between the candle and its image.

title: GCSE Physics - Reflection
why: Cognito on the normal, the two angles and where a mirror image ends up, beside our own worked steps.

prompt: An object stands 15 cm in front of a plane mirror. How far behind the mirror does its image appear, in cm?
explain: 15 cm. The mirror sits exactly halfway between the object and its image, so the image is as far behind as the object is in front.

twin.prompt: A vase stands 21 cm in front of a plane mirror. How far behind the mirror does its image appear, in cm?
twin.explain: 21 cm: the image stands behind the mirror by the same distance the vase stands in front.

prompt: What makes the image in a plane mirror virtual rather than real?
options: no light actually arrives at the place the image appears to be
the image is smaller than the object
answer: no light actually arrives at the place the image appears to be
explain: No light gets behind the mirror. Your brain traces the rays back to a point where nothing is, which is exactly what virtual means. Size and which way up it is are separate properties.

optionNotes.option: the image is smaller than the object
optionNotes.why: A plane-mirror image matches the object in size, and size has nothing to do with whether an image is real or virtual.
A plane-mirror image is upright, and which way up it is does not decide real or virtual.

twin.prompt: Why could a screen held behind a plane mirror never catch its image?
options: no light passes behind the mirror to reach it
the image is too faint to show on a screen
twin.answer: no light passes behind the mirror to reach it
twin.explain: The image is virtual: the rays only seem to come from behind the mirror, and no light ever gets there, so a screen would stay blank.

optionNotes.option: the image is too faint to show on a screen
optionNotes.why: Brightness is not the reason: no light at all reaches the place behind the mirror.
Lateral inversion is about left and right; it does not stop light reaching a screen. The image is virtual.

md: A ray can reflect from one mirror onto a second. Each mirror has **its own normal**. When the mirrors are at **right angles**, their normals are at right angles too, so the ray's angle to the first normal and its angle to the second **add up to 90°**.

stem: Two plane mirrors are fixed at right angles. A ray hits mirror A with an angle of incidence of 64°. Find its angle of incidence at mirror B. [3]

steps.working: At mirror A the ray leaves at 64° to A's normal.
steps.decision: The law of reflection at the first mirror.

steps.working: Mirror B is at right angles to A, so B's normal is at right angles to A's normal.
steps.decision: Each mirror has its own normal; the two meet at 90°.

steps.working: The ray makes 90° − 64° = 26° with B's normal: that is the angle of incidence at B.
steps.decision: The two angles of incidence add up to 90°.

prompt: Two plane mirrors are fixed at right angles. A ray hits mirror A with an angle of incidence of 57°. What is its angle of incidence at mirror B, in degrees?
explain: 90° − 57° = 33°. The two normals are at right angles, so the two angles of incidence always add up to 90°.

twin.prompt: The same two mirrors: a ray hits mirror A with an angle of incidence of 71°. What is its angle of incidence at mirror B, in degrees?
twin.explain: 90° − 71° = 19°: the angles at the two mirrors add up to 90°.

md: **Arrows on rays.** A mark goes on the arrow of the reflected ray, pointing away from the mirror; Summer 2023 and Summer 2024 Foundation examiners saw it left off or pointed at the mirror. **Ray along the normal.** A ray that arrives along the normal has an angle of incidence of 0°, not 90°, and goes straight back. **Ticked properties.** Tick one of each pair: real and virtual together cancel.

stem: A printed diagram shows a ray reaching a plane mirror, with its angle of incidence of 40° marked. Label the normal and complete the reflected ray. [3]

steps.working: Label the dashed line at right angles to the mirror as the normal.
steps.decision: The normal is what every angle is measured from; examiners give it a mark.

steps.working: Draw the reflected ray at 40° to the normal, on the other side of it.
steps.decision: Use a protractor from the normal, not from the mirror.

steps.working: Put an arrow on the reflected ray, pointing away from the mirror.
steps.decision: The arrow shows the direction the light travels.

prompt: A student ticks both real and virtual to describe the image in a plane mirror. What does that pair earn?
options: nothing: the two contradict each other and cancel
one mark, for the right word
two marks, one for each word
answer: nothing: the two contradict each other and cancel
explain: Real and virtual contradict each other, so examiners cancel the pair: tick one word from each pair. Summer 2023 Foundation examiners saw a few tick real and virtual together.

optionNotes.option: one mark, for the right word
optionNotes.why: A right word beside its opposite is cancelled, not credited: choose one of the pair.

optionNotes.option: two marks, one for each word
optionNotes.why: Only one of the two can be true; together they cancel, so the pair earns nothing.

twin.prompt: A student writes that a mirror image is both upright and upside down. What does that pair earn?
twin.explain: Upright and upside down contradict each other, so the pair earns nothing; the image is upright.

optionNotes.why: Upright is right, but written beside its opposite it is cancelled.
A plane-mirror image is upright, and a contradictory pair earns nothing anyway.

md:
Draw the normal before anything else, and measure both angles from it.
Use the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, turning an angle to the surface into one to the normal first.
Describe the image: virtual, upright, same size, laterally inverted, as far behind as the object is in front.
Work out the second angle when two mirrors are at right angles.

A printed diagram with a mark for each part: label the normal, complete the reflected ray, put the arrow on it, then state an angle. Image properties come as a tick list or a short answer, where two contradictory ticks cancel out. Stuck? Draw the normal first, then measure both angles from it.
